blocks.text: Some tools answer in a blink. Others take real time, a search across a huge codebase, a call to a slow external API, a video or file conversion that chugs along for minutes.
If a client just sits there waiting silently for one of these slow tools, the whole session can feel frozen, even though work is actually happening.
This lesson looks at why some tools are slow, why blocking is a real problem, and the patterns MCP uses so a client can stay responsive and keep the user informed.
1. Why Some Tools Take a While

blocks.alt: A quick tool returns fast while a slow tool takes real time to run

blocks.text: A tool is just a function the server exposes, and like any function, some versions of it do more work than others.
A search tool might need to scan millions of rows or files before it can return anything useful.
A tool that calls out to a third party API is at the mercy of that other service, which might be slow, rate limited, or briefly overloaded.
A file conversion tool, turning a video into a different format for example, does real computational work that simply takes time no matter how well it is written.

blocks.title: Slow is not broken
blocks.content: A tool taking thirty seconds is not a bug, it is just doing real work. The problem is only how that wait is handled, not the wait itself.

blocks.text: 2. The Blocking Call Problem

blocks.alt: A blocking call freezes the client while waiting for the tool to finish

blocks.text: In the simplest possible design, a client sends a tools/call request and just waits for the response before doing anything else.
For a fast tool this is fine, the wait is so short nobody notices it.
For a slow tool, that same wait can stretch to seconds or minutes, and during that whole time the client has nothing new to show.
Worse, if the client is single threaded or tied to one session, that one slow call can block everything else the user might want to do.

items: The user cannot cancel or redirect the request mid flight.
The user gets no sense of whether the tool is stuck or simply slow.
Other unrelated work in the same session may have to wait too.
A truly stuck call can hang the client forever with no clear signal.

blocks.text: 3. Synchronous Feel, Asynchronous Reality
MCP tool calls are still requests that eventually get one final result, so from a protocol standpoint they look synchronous, one call, one matching response.
But underneath, a server is free to treat a call asynchronously internally, doing the work in steps and reporting on those steps as they happen.
The trick is a separate channel, progress notifications, that flow alongside the pending request instead of forcing the client to sit in silence.

blocks.title: Notifications, not responses
blocks.content: A progress notification is a one way message. It does not complete the tool call, the final tools/call result still arrives on its own later.

blocks.text: 4. The progressToken Parameter

blocks.alt: A progress token attached to a call lets the server report progress

blocks.text: To get progress updates for a specific call, the client attaches a progressToken inside the request metadata when it sends tools/call.
That token is just an identifier the client picked, a string or number unique enough to match later notifications back to this one call.
If the client leaves progressToken out, it is telling the server it does not want progress updates for this particular call.
5. Sending a Progress Notification

blocks.alt: The server sends a progress notification while the tool keeps running

blocks.text: Once a server sees a progressToken on an in flight call, it can send notifications/progress messages while the work continues.
Each message carries the same progressToken so the client knows exactly which pending call it belongs to.
A server can send as many of these as it wants, spaced however makes sense for the task, no fixed schedule is required.
6. Structuring a Progress Payload
The progress field is a number that should increase over time, and total, when known, gives the client a denominator to compute a percentage.
Sometimes total is not known in advance, a search might have no idea how many results it will eventually find.
In that case a server can send progress without a total, and the client falls back to showing an indeterminate spinner rather than a percentage bar.

blocks.text: 7. Writing an Async Tool Handler
On the server side, a tool handler that expects to run long simply reports progress at natural checkpoints inside its own work loop.
Notice the handler only sends notifications when a progressToken was actually provided, it never forces progress updates on a client that did not ask for them.
8. The Same Pattern in Python
The exact same idea works in any language a server happens to be written in, the shape of the loop just changes slightly.
9. Timeouts: Why They Matter

blocks.alt: A tool without a timeout can hang the whole conversation

blocks.text: Progress updates help a client stay informed, but they do not solve every problem, a tool can still get truly stuck, not just slow.
A timeout is a limit a client sets on how long it will wait for a tool call before giving up entirely.
Without a timeout, one hung external API call could tie up a session forever, waiting on a response that may simply never come.

blocks.title: Timeouts protect the client, not the server
blocks.content: A timeout is a client side decision. The server might still finish the work, the client is just choosing to stop waiting for it.

blocks.text: 10. Setting a Timeout for a Tool Call
A client typically picks a timeout value when it sends the request, and resets that timer each time a fresh progress notification arrives for that call.
This pattern only times out a call that has gone quiet, a tool that is actively reporting progress gets more patience than one that has gone silent.
11. What Happens When a Timeout Fires

blocks.alt: A timeout firing cancels the tool call and returns an error

blocks.text: When a client decides a call has taken too long, it typically sends a cancellation notification for that request rather than just abandoning it silently.
A well behaved server sees this, stops the underlying work if it can, and simply does not bother sending a final result for that request anymore.
The client, on its side, stops waiting immediately once it has sent the cancellation, it does not need to wait for a matching response.
12. Cancellation and Cleanup

blocks.alt: A cancelled tool call still needs to release its resources during cleanup

blocks.text: A tool that might run long should be written so it can be interrupted cleanly, not just left to run to completion regardless.
This often means checking a cancellation flag between chunks of work, and releasing any resources, open files, network connections, temporary data, as soon as it notices the call was cancelled.

items: Check a cancellation signal between steps of a loop, not only at the very start.
Close any open files, sockets, or database cursors before exiting early.
Avoid leaving partially written output behind that could confuse a later run.
Log the cancellation so the operator can tell it apart from a normal failure.

blocks.text: 13. How a Client Shows Ongoing Work
The whole point of progress notifications is wasted if the client just throws them away, the interface needs to actually reflect them.
A chat style client might turn each progress message into an updating status line, scanning page 4 of 12, right below the pending tool call.
A more visual client could turn the progress and total fields into an actual moving progress bar.
14. Handling Tools With No Progress Support
Not every tool reports progress, some are just too simple to bother, others were written before this pattern was considered.
A client cannot assume progress notifications are guaranteed, so it needs a fallback for a call that goes quiet but has not technically timed out yet.
A generic spinner with a rough elapsed time counter is a reasonable fallback, it at least tells the user something is still happening.

blocks.title: Set expectations honestly
blocks.content: If a tool has no progress reporting, a good client still avoids implying false precision, a plain still working message beats a fake percentage.

blocks.text: 15. Designing Long Running Tools Well
When building a tool you expect to be slow, break the work into natural chunks up front, this makes reporting progress and honoring cancellation both much easier.
Pick a reasonable frequency for progress messages, too rare and the client looks frozen between them, too frequent and you flood the connection with noise.
Always include a human readable message alongside the raw numbers, a user reads scanning page 4 of 12 far more easily than a bare progress value.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Picture a tool called summarize_report that reads a large PDF and produces a summary, a task that realistically takes about a minute.
The client calls it with a progressToken and a sixty second timeout.
The client resets its timeout clock on each of those three progress messages, so the slow but healthy call never gets cancelled by mistake.
If page 31 had instead gone silent for a full minute, the timeout would fire and the client would send a cancellation notification instead of waiting forever.
Common Mistakes

items: Blocking the whole client on a slow tool call instead of letting other work continue.
Forgetting to attach a progressToken, then wondering why no progress notifications ever arrive.
Sending progress updates so frequently that they flood the connection with noise.
Ignoring cancellation notifications and letting an abandoned tool keep running anyway.
Setting a timeout so short that normal, healthy slow tools get cancelled constantly.
Showing a fake precise percentage when the tool actually has no idea how much work remains.

blocks.text: Practice
Design progress reporting for a tool called resize_images that resizes 200 photos one at a time, taking roughly ten minutes total.
Key Takeaway
Slow tools are normal, the real risk is a client that sits frozen with no signal that work is even happening.
Progress notifications tied to a progressToken, paired with sensible timeouts and clean cancellation, let a client stay responsive and keep the user confidently informed the whole time.
